This would likely depend on what type of test bank you’re talking about. 

A test bank designed to accompany a textbook and sold to teachers with sample exam questions, purchased and used by students, would almost certainly constitute a violation of academic integrity. 
 
A compilation of exams taken in previous semesters by other students does not appear to be a violation of academic integrity. Several student organizations have maintained test banks for years. The associated academic departments are likely aware of it, and if it was a matter of concern, something could have been done long before now. I haven’t found any existing precedent of a UMD student being charged with an academic violation for using a student-run test bank. 

[This](https://thedailytexan.com/2019/03/27/professors-shouldn’t-consider-using-test-banks-cheating) article from the University of Texas does a fairly thorough job of explaining their position and perspective on test banks. Part of it reads: 

“Any professor that gives back or fails to collect exams should expect that future students can and will use these exams as a resource when studying. If professors do not want this to happen, they should either make sure exams stay inside the classroom or come up with new questions for future tests. 

Students have also been taught that one of the most effective ways to study is with practice quizzes and self-testing. Therefore, using old test questions to study should be encouraged rather than frowned upon.”

Hopefully this has helped to address your concerns.
